title: How the Community Learning Centre is helping adult learners achieve Sustainable Success
summary: A story of how the Hogoro Community Learning Centre combines literacy and ecological farming to help adult learners improve confidence, productivity and community life.

author.name: Joseph Masonda
author.role: Communications Officer | Digital Marketer | Website Designer | Content Creator | AI Enthusiast | Framer Developer | Writer

content.text: Community Learning Centres (CLCs) are grassroots institutions that provide services and learning opportunities for adults, out-of-school children, young people and illiterate or semi-literate adults from socially disadvantaged communities. DVV International supports the ICBAE programme, functional literacy and CLC strengthening in pilot areas in Dodoma (Kongwa and Mpwapwa) and the Coastal Region (Kisarawe and Kibaha).

Adult education programmes in CLCs provide training in skills development, livelihoods and agriculture that is crucial for community sustainability. They go beyond basic reading and writing by improving livelihoods, helping rural communities make informed choices and take control of their personal and collective lives.
When adult education is linked closely to development activities, learners can improve their daily work, strengthen their capabilities and increase their quality of life.

Adult learners often prioritise education that relates directly to their livelihoods. In Hogoro Ward in Kongwa District, Dodoma Region, many community members were limited by inability to read and write, alongside low farm productivity caused by inadequate knowledge of sustainable farming practices.

High soil salinity, low yields and deteriorating soil quality had trapped farmers in a cycle of poverty. Traditional farming methods could no longer sustain them. Without training, many could not access new approaches or even follow written instructions.

For farmers Livingstone Ndalu and Michael Mataluma, the Hogoro Community Learning Centre became a symbol of hope and change. Established and launched in July 2023 by DVV International in collaboration with Kongwa District Council, the centre integrates functional literacy, skills development and vocational training.
According to CLC coordinator Jackson Mdima, since the project began in December 2022, it had reached 217 participants in 16 groups: 77 men and 140 women.

Livingstone and Michael are part of the Mshikamano Group, taught by community facilitator Merry Mbogoni. They take literacy classes and participate in hands-on sustainable agriculture training using a demonstration garden at the centre. Organisations including MVIWATA, Seedland Ltd, Farm Africa and Farm Radio (Mkulima Mbunifu) provide training in agriculture and entrepreneurship.

The training focuses on climate-resilient, sustainable practices that support productivity. The demonstration garden is both a practical learning space and a source of income to support small CLC operations.

After joining literacy classes in August 2023, Livingstone and Michael, who had initially been unable to read or write, made considerable progress. Within three months, both had become literate. The classes gave them confidence to participate more actively in community life.

They were also introduced to ecological farming techniques, including appropriate use of fertiliser, composting and selection of suitable local seeds. Applying these techniques on the demonstration plot reinforced their learning and delivered immediate benefits.

Michael, who had initially been reluctant to admit his illiteracy, now reads and writes proudly and contributes to his community with greater confidence. His adoption of ecological farming practices changed his approach to agriculture.
We used to farm for three months, and harvesting was done within three weeks. Now, we are currently harvesting up to six months.

The economic impact is also visible. Michael’s tomato harvest increased from 20–30 bags to 200 bags, illustrating the connection between functional literacy, improved agricultural practices and productivity. The result has improved economic stability and quality of life, while encouraging other community members to join the CLC.

Livingstone and Michael have become programme champions, teaching others and sharing the benefits of literacy and sustainable farming. Their journey illustrates how education and skills development can produce meaningful change.

The CLC is also a source of news and information for the community. It has a television and speakers for announcements, allowing residents without television access to follow news, sport and entertainment. Advertisements and community announcements are broadcast through the speakers, keeping people informed and connected.

Their story shows how knowledge, skills and sustainable practices can change lives. At the Hogoro CLC, learners gain literacy and agricultural knowledge while the centre gives the community a place to come together, share information and learn. The initiative demonstrates how communities can overcome poverty and build a more sustainable future when they have appropriate support and resources.
The success of the CLC in Hogoro shows how adult education can drive development and enable people to make positive changes in their lives and communities.
